'''Leonard Reiffel''' (September 30, 1927 – April 15, 2017) was an American physicist, author and educator. Born in Chicago, Reiffel was an electrical engineering student for a number of years before entering into research fields. He collaborated with [[Enrico Fermi]], [[Carl Sagan]], and members of [[Operation Paperclip]].

Reiffel also worked for [[NASA]] and the [[Illinois Institute of Technology]], and won a [[Peabody Award]] for his work on the radio program ''The World Tomorrow''. His experience with broadcasting led him to invent the [[telestrator]] as a visual aid for his programming; Reiffel held over fifty different patents for his inventions.

==Early life==

Reiffel was born in Chicago on September 30, 1927.{{sfn|Kalte|Nemeh|2003|p=122}} His father was Carl Reiffel, a silversmith credited with inventing a slide saxophone. His mother, the former Sophie Miller, was a district superintendent in the Chicago public school system.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/04/26/us/obituary-leonard-reiffel-nuclear-bomb-moon.html|title=Leonard Reiffel, Who Studied Potential of a Lunar Nuclear Bomb, Dies at 89 |first=Richard |last=Sandomir |date=April 26, 2017 |work=[[The New York Times]] |access-date=April 27, 2017 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20170427073159/https://www.nytimes.com/2017/04/26/us/obituary-leonard-reiffel-nuclear-bomb-moon.html?_r=0 |archive-date=April 27, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> The younger Reiffel attended [[Theodore Roosevelt High School (Chicago, Illinois)|Theodore Roosevelt High School]], before earning a bachelor's and master's degree as well as a doctorate in electrical engineering from the [[Illinois Institute of Technology]] between 1947 and 1953.<ref name="crain"/>

==Career==

=== Universities and inventions===

Reiffel began his career at the [[University of Chicago]]'s [[Enrico Fermi Institute|Institute for Nuclear Studies]], helping [[Enrico Fermi]] construct a 450-inch [[cyclotron]].<ref name="AIP"/> From there, Reiffel returned to the university at which he had studied, the Illinois Institute of Technology. Here, Reiffel was Group Vice President of the [[IIT Research Institute]] (formerly known as the Armour Research Foundation). During his tenure at the university, Reiffel created and patented over fifty different inventions, which earned him four separate R&D 100 Awards.<ref name="AIP"/><ref name="R&D">{{cite web |url=http://www.rdmag.com/RD100SearchResults.aspx?strDeveloper=reiffel&Type=D |title=R&D Mag |publisher=R&D Magazine |access-date=September 28, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120405220113/http://www.rdmag.com/RD100SearchResults.aspx?strDeveloper=reiffel&Type=D |archive-date=April 5, 2012 |url-status=dead  }}</ref> Reiffel also collaborated with German scientists recruited in America as part of [[Operation Paperclip]], working on an early prototype for a [[railgun]].<ref name="crain"/>

===NASA===
Reiffel was involved in several positions in NASA's [[Apollo program]], moving from being a consultant on the possibility of life on the Moon<ref name="peabody">{{cite web |url=http://www.peabody.uga.edu/winners/details.php?id=805 |title=The Peabody Awards {{!}} An International Competition for Electronic Media, honoring achievement in Television, Radio, Cable and the Web |publisher=[[Henry W. Grady College of Journalism and Mass Communication]] |access-date=September 27, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330232321/http://www.peabody.uga.edu/winners/details.php?id=805 |archive-date=March 30, 2012 |url-status=dead  }}</ref> to become deputy director of the project,<ref name="IIT">{{cite web |url=http://www.iit.edu/about/history/hall_of_fame/leonard_reiffel.shtml |title=About IIT {{!}} Hall of Fame {{!}} Leonard Reiffel |publisher=[[Illinois Institute of Technology]] |date=September 7, 2011 |access-date=September 28, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110118051040/http://www.iit.edu/about/history/hall_of_fame/leonard_reiffel.shtml |archive-date=January 18, 2011 |url-status=dead }}</ref> a post he held from 1965 to 1969.<ref name="AIP">{{cite web |url=http://www.aip.org/history/historymatters/reiffel.htm |title=Leonard Reiffel |publisher=[[American Institute of Physics]] |access-date=September 28, 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110821133705/http://www.aip.org/history/historymatters/reiffel.htm |archive-date=August 21, 2011 |url-status=dead  }}</ref> During this time, Reiffel was also put in charge of [[Project A119]], a [[United States Air Force]] project intending to detonate a nuclear warhead on the Moon. Reiffel worked alongside [[Carl Sagan]] and [[Gerard Kuiper]] on the project.<ref name="Guardian">{{cite news| url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2000/may/14/spaceexploration.theobserver |title=US planned one big nuclear blast for mankind |newspaper=[[The Guardian]] |date=May 14, 2000 |first=Antony |last=Barnett |access-date=September 8, 2011}}</ref>{{sfn|Ulivi|Harland|2004|pp=19–21}} Reiffel also chaired the Interagency Manned Space Flight Experiments Board for several years, a body which worked alongside NASA, the United States Air Force, and the [[United States Department of Defense]].<ref name="AIP"/>

===Broadcasting===

Reiffel's work on radio and television has included ''Backyard Safari'', ''Dimensions on Tomorrow's Living'' and ''The World Tomorrow''.<ref name="AIP"/> ''Backyard Safari'' was nominated for an [[Emmy Award]],<ref name="AIP"/> whilst Reiffel was honored with a [[Peabody Award]] in 1968 for his work on ''The World Tomorrow''.<ref name="peabody"/> Reiffel's time as a broadcaster led to him developing the [[telestrator]], a device for drawing over still or moving video images; the device is now commonly employed by [[American football]] broadcasters while discussing [[Play from scrimmage|plays]].<ref name="crain"/> Reiffel first used the telestrator as part of ''Backyard Safari'' before convincing [[WBBM-TV]] weatherman [[John Coughlin (weatherman)|John Coughlin]] to use it as part of his forecasts; it was from there that sports anchor [[Johnny Morris (American football)|Johnny Morris]] introduced its use to sports broadcasting.<ref name="tribune obit"/>

===Other work===

Reiffel also worked as an artwork authenticator for the [[Hermitage Museum]] in [[Saint Petersburg]], investigating the authenticity of work by [[Édouard Manet]] in 2002.<ref name="crain">{{cite news |title=From the moon to the end zone; This inventor helped run NASA, split atoms with Fermi, and even changed the way we watch football. And he's not done yet |author=Johnsson, Julie |newspaper=[[Crain's Chicago Business]] |date=October 14, 2002 }} {{subscription required}}</ref> In 1979, he published the science fiction novel ''The Contaminant''.<ref name="tribune obit"/> He also acted as a consultant to the governments of [[Belarus]] and [[Ukraine]] following the [[Chernobyl incident]]; this experience led him to write an unpublished second novel about nuclear terrorism.<ref name="crain"/>

==Death==

Reiffel died of complications from pancreatic cancer in Chicago on April 15, 2017. He was survived by his second wife Nancy Reiffel, and sons Evan and David.<ref name="tribune obit">{{cite web |url=http://www.chicagotribune.com/news/obituaries/ct-leonard-reiffel-obituary-20170420-story.html |title=Leonard Reiffel, inventor of telestrator used to show NFL replays, dies at 89 |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |first=Bob |last=Goldsborough |date=April 20, 2017 |access-date=April 20, 2017}}</ref>
